extracted.intended_audience: regulatory analysts, OSHA staff, small business representatives, SBREFA panel participants, and stakeholders evaluating economic impacts of the proposed OSHA heat standard
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic criteria for assessing whether the proposed OSHA heat standard would have a significant economic impact on small and very small entities, using cost-to-revenue screening tests, average annualized costs, and related procedural steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-to-revenue screening threshold (1%)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA relies on a screening test—costs less than one percent of revenue—to evaluate the impacts on small and very small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the cost-to-revenue ratio (average compliance cost as a percent of revenue) for an industry is below 1%, OSHA treats the costs as unlikely to threaten survival of small entities or alter competitive structure. The 1% threshold is the primary screening test applied to establishments of all sizes and to small/very small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of average compliance costs per affected small and very small entity
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA examines the average compliance costs per affected small entity and very small entity for each industry covered under the final standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute average annualized compliance cost per entity and compare to average revenue per entity to derive cost as percent of revenue; see Section VIII.B. for methodology and the tables (VIII.D.2 and VIII.D.3) presenting these averages for NAICS industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Further investigation when screening threshold exceeded
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases where the small and very small entities in particular industries are above the threshold level for the primary screening test, OSHA will investigate further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceeding the 1% threshold does not automatically mean the standard is infeasible; it triggers additional analysis to determine whether impacts are concentrated, marginal, or likely to alter industry structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of alteration of competitive structure
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA evaluates whether the competitive structure of an industry could be significantly altered (for example, if most or all small firms in that industry would have to close).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If compliance costs would force most or all small firms to close, OSHA may conclude the competitive structure is affected. This assessment relies on estimated average costs and patterns across firms in the industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) determination requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA is required by the Regulatory Flexibility Act to determine whether a proposed standard would likely have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As part of the Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis, OSHA performs a screening analysis of costs as a percentage of revenues and reports results (e.g., number of industries above the 1% threshold) to satisfy RFA obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of diseconomies of scale for small businesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Smaller businesses typically suffer from diseconomies of scale, leading to lower revenue per dollar of cost and higher average costs compared with larger establishments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA acknowledges higher average cost impacts for small entities but notes small firms may mitigate disadvantages by specializing, offering local/better service, or being more dynamic. OSHA compares observed impacts to ranges from prior standards and looks for evidence of industry failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs primarily employee-based (not establishment-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis notes that compliance costs for this standard are overwhelmingly employee-based rather than establishment-based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because costs are per-employee, the general profile of impacts does not differ significantly between small and larger entities, reducing the likelihood of unique challenges for small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of SBREFA input and regulatory alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA considered input from SBA-defined small entities who participated in the SBREFA process and adjusted the regulatory framework accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA drafted and analyzed a set of regulatory alternatives and options in response to SBAR Panel recommendations; the agency documents these adjustments in the Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (Section VIII.F.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological convention: annualized costs using 2% discount rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The economic impact tables present annualized costs calculated using a 2% discount rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables report total annualized costs, average annualized cost per entity, average revenue per entity, and costs as percent of revenue. The 2% discount rate is the convention used in the presented calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision inference from industry counts and marginal exceedances
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA uses the distribution of industry-level cost-to-revenue ratios (e.g., how many of 298 NAICS industries exceed 1%) to support conclusions about feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only a small number of industries exceed the screening threshold and impacts are marginal, OSHA concludes compliance would be feasible for small entities and unlikely to alter industry structure; specific industries with marginally higher ratios are identified and discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution of higher costs to lagging employers
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA indicates that costs will be borne primarily by businesses that have lagged in implementing safety measures (those that did not invest earlier to reduce heat exposure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may consider that firms which have already incurred preventive investments will face lower incremental costs; this context affects judgments about which firms are at risk and whether industry-wide competitive effects are likely.
